findings.title: Confirmation dialog orphaning: NSAlert survives task cancellation with degraded execution fallback
evidence: Step 1: User invokes Flyd with a consequential intent (e.g., 'send this email'). Core returns mode='native' with requiresConfirmation=true or the executor flags a destructive replacement.
Step 2: processInvocation() enters the case 'native': branch at line 604. ConfirmationDecision.reasons is non-empty, so decision.requiresConfirmation is true.

Step 3: requestCombinedConfirmation() at line 788 creates an NSAlert and calls runModal(), which starts a nested NSRunLoop on the main thread. The processInvocation Task awaits the withCheckedContinuation.
Step 4: Before the user clicks Allow/Cancel, they press the fn key (triggered by handleShortcutPress if state.phase != .idle, or handleInvocation if currentPhase != .idle).

Step 5: handleShortcutPress() at line 416 fires: activeInvocationTask?.cancel() sets the cooperative cancellation flag on the Task; state.cancelInvocation() sets mode=present, phase=idle, invocationId=nil; stateMachine.cancel() calls resetCheckpoints() which nils t1Fingerprint; invocationPanel.dismiss() removes the invocation panel.
Step 6: The NSAlert remains visible — nothing in handleShortcutPress() dismisses it. The user sees a confirmation dialog for a cancelled invocation.

Step 7a: If user clicks 'Allow': the continuation resumes with confirmed=true. The guard at line 623 passes. executeNativeOperations() at line 638 is called. Inside, verifyPreExecution() at line 726 returns false (t1Fingerprint was nilled by resetCheckpoints). Text goes to clipboard as fallback. Outcome 'failed' is sent to Core.

Step 7b: If user clicks 'Cancel': the continuation resumes with confirmed=false. guard fails. Outcome 'rejected' sent. invocationPanel.dismiss() called on already-dismissed panel (harmless but noisy).

Step 8: In both cases, processInvocation continues past line 703 into audit/clear/reset/transition. state.transition(to: .present) is called but state is already .present (from cancelInvocation in Step 5). executor.clearInvocationRefs() and stateMachine.resetCheckpoints() are called again — redundant but harmless.

Root cause: requestCombinedConfirmation() at line 788 has no cancellation-awareness. The NSAlert runModal() creates a nested event loop that ignores Task cancellation. There is no check for Task.isCancelled inside the native branch after the confirmation await or before executeNativeOperations.
findings.scenario: Consequence: The user is confronted with an orphaned modal dialog after cancelling an invocation. While verifyPreExecution() prevents unauthorized text insertion (the text goes to clipboard instead), the UX is confusing and the state machine transitions are inconsistent. More critically: if future operation kinds (e.g., file operations, network requests) are added that don't check verifyPreExecution(), this orphaning pattern becomes a confirmation-bypass vector.

findings.title: AugmentPanel rendered on wrong monitor due to NSScreen.main in multi-display setups
evidence: showAugmentations() at line 362: guard let screen = NSScreen.main else { return }
NSScreen.main returns the screen containing the key window. Flyd runs with NSApp.setActivationPolicy(.accessory), which means it has no visible menu bar and its key window behavior is unpredictable.

On a MacBook with an external display: if Flyd's last interaction was on the built-in display (e.g., setup window, status menu click), NSScreen.main resolves to the built-in display even when the user is working on the external monitor.

centerX and centerY at lines 368-369 are computed from screen.visibleFrame. The anchor at line 371 uses centerX. If the wrong screen is selected, the entire stacked panel layout is positioned on the wrong monitor — potentially offscreen if the external monitor has a different resolution or offset.

visibleFrame differs per screen: internal display has menu bar at top (visibleFrame.origin.y ≈ 0, height ≈ screenHeight - 22). External display typically has visibleFrame == frame (no menu bar). The Y-offset mismatch means panels can render behind or above the visible area.

The stackedFrames() function at line 32 clamps each frame to screenVisibleFrame, but the screenVisibleFrame parameter is from the wrong screen. Clamping to the wrong screen's bounds doesn't help when the anchor point is entirely on a different display.
findings.scenario: Concrete reproduction: MacBook Pro (1728x1117) + 27-inch external display (2560x1440, right of built-in). User works in Safari on external display, invokes Flyd. NSScreen.main returns built-in display because the status menu click registered there. Augment panes compute center from built-in's visibleFrame (centered at ~864, ~530) and appear on the wrong screen — invisible from the external display.

findings.title: TTS endpoint: unbounded memory allocation from OpenAI response with no size validation
evidence: synthesizeSpeech() at line 48: const arrayBuffer = await response.arrayBuffer(); return Buffer.from(arrayBuffer); reads the ENTIRE response body into memory with no size limit.

While the input text is capped at MAX_TTS_CHARS=4000 (line 15), there is no guarantee that OpenAI's API response is proportional to input size. A 4000-char input could theoretically produce multi-MB AAC audio.
The fetch at line 22 uses AbortSignal.timeout(15_000) which limits total request duration, but a fast connection could deliver gigabytes in 15 seconds.

The Core HTTP server at line 83 constrains manifest body size (MANIFEST_BODY_LIMIT = 4MB), but there is no equivalent limit on the TTS response path. The response is streamed back to the Swift adapter via res.end(audio) with Content-Length audio.length — Node.js will buffer the entire response.
The Swift adapter's FlydClient.speak() at line 252 reads the data into a Data object (another full copy in memory), then SpeechPlayer plays it via AVAudioPlayer(data:). This is a third allocation.
A compromised or misconfigured upstream (MITM proxy, modified DNS, compromised CDN) could return arbitrarily large body from what appears to be api.openai.com.
findings.scenario: Attack: an attacker with network-position advantage intercepts the HTTPS connection (corporate proxy, local root CA) and returns a 200 OK with Content-Type: audio/aac and a 2GB body. Core's Node.js process allocates 2GB for the response → OOM crash. Even without malice: a legitimate OpenAI API anomaly (e.g., content-length mismatch, chunked encoding issue) could produce unexpected response sizes.

findings.title: LIVE: WebSocket server silent failure after startup — runtime errors go unhandled
evidence: startRealtimeServer() at line 37 creates a WebSocketServer with wss.on('error', reject) at line 53. This only attaches an error handler during the promise-construction phase.

After the 'listening' event fires at line 48, the promise resolves and is never rejected again. The 'error' event handler (set at line 53) remains attached but the promise's reject function can no longer be called (the promise is already resolved).

If a runtime error occurs after listening (e.g., OS socket buffer exhaustion, EMFILE from too many connections, TLS handshake failure if that were supported), the error event fires but is swallowed — no log, no crash, no recovery.
The connection handler at line 55 handles individual connection errors (via the ws 'message' try/catch at line 90), but server-level errors have no handler after startup.
startServer() at line 530-535 in server.ts: if LIVE_ENABLED, startRealtimeServer() is called with a .catch() that logs the warning. But after the initial success, no further error monitoring exists.

wss.on('connection', ...) is the only event registered after error. If the server enters a bad state (e.g., half-closed socket from a kernel-level issue), no event fires and the server silently degrades.
findings.scenario: Concrete scenario: LIVE_ENABLED=true, server starts successfully on port 4817. After hours of operation, the macOS kernel hits a socket table limit. A new connection attempt triggers an 'error' event on the WSS instance. The error handler fires but the reject function is a no-op (promise already resolved). No log message, no status change, no restart. The server appears running but silently drops all new connections. Meanwhile, the health check at /health returns 'ok' because it doesn't check the WS server state.

findings.title: processInvocation: no cancellation check after confirmation await — stale continuation executes past Task cancellation
evidence: The only Task.isCancelled guard in processInvocation is at line 562-568, BEFORE the switch(resolution.mode) block.

After entering case 'native': at line 605, there are zero checks for Task.isCancelled. The logic proceeds through: confirmation decision building (606-618), await requestCombinedConfirmation (619), execution (638), voice reply (654-663), audit (703-707), state cleanup (712-717).

If the Task is cancelled while awaiting requestCombinedConfirmation (e.g., handleShortcutPress at line 420 calls activeInvocationTask?.cancel()), the NSAlert continuation still resumes. The code at lines 623-717 all execute despite the Task being cancelled.

The guard at line 562-568 was designed to catch cancellation 'during resolution', which makes sense for the API call. But the confirmation dialog is a new async suspension point — a new cancellation opportunity — with no corresponding guard.

Contrast with the voice flow: cleanupVoiceInvocation() at line 405 calls activeInvocationTask?.cancel() explicitly, and the onComplete/onError callbacks on the voice relay check state.phase before proceeding. The text flow has no equivalent.

While verifyPreExecution() blocks actual text insertion (see ADV-001), the outcome-sending (line 624/756), state transitions (line 717), and audit recording (line 703) all execute on a cancelled Task, producing spurious side effects.
findings.scenario: Minimal fix: add guard Task.isCancelled after the await requestCombinedConfirmation() call. If cancelled, return early without executing operations. Additionally, dismiss the NSAlert (it needs its own reference for programmatic dismissal, which it currently lacks).

findings.title: AugmentPanel rapid-fire: global monitor proliferation with no per-instance lifecycle bound
evidence: Each AugmentPanel.show() call at line 218 registers NSEvent.addGlobalMonitorForEvents(matching: .leftMouseDown) — a system-wide tap that Apple limits (undocumented but observed: ~10-20 per process before silent failure).

showAugmentations() at line 359 dismisses old panels (which removes their monitors via dismiss() line 251-254), then creates new panels (which register new monitors). This is serialized on MainActor, so the old monitors are removed before new ones are added — safe for sequential calls.

However, the 0.35s entrance animation at line 230 runs asynchronously via NSAnimationContext.runAnimationGroup. If showAugmentations is called again during this animation window, dismiss() on the old panel may teardown its views (including clipView.layer) while CALayer animations are in flight. This produces a Core Animation 'implicit animation removed' warning but no crash.

The 30-second autoDismissTimer at line 222 is a repeating risk: if AugmentPanel instances accumulate (multiple rapid invocations each creating panels that don't trigger click-to-dismiss), timers could build up. But each new showAugmentations call dismisses old panels (invalidating timers), and click-to-dismiss removes them. In practice, only user-inactivity could accumulate timers.

No hard cap on active panels: line 374 maps augmentations to AugmentPanel instances 1:1 with no limit. If Core returns 50 augmentations (unlikely due to prompt constraints but possible if the LLM hallucinates), 50 NSPanels + 50 global monitors + 50 timers are created simultaneously.
findings.scenario: The immediate risk is low because prompt constraints limit augmentations to ~4 and MainActor serialization prevents race. The residual risk: if the LLM returns an excessive number of augmentations or if showAugmentations is called externally (e.g., from a future API endpoint), there is no defense-in-depth cap.

residual_risks: Codable migration: decodeIfPresent gracefully handles type mismatches by returning nil (all fields fall back to defaults), but a malicious config file that intentionally corrupts all fields could silently reset every user preference to defaults. The user would notice their settings were lost but would not know why.

Voice transcription timeout: startVoiceTranscriptionTimeout() sets a 20s timeout, but the Core-side transcription.ts transcribeBufferedAudio() at line 224-235 loops through fallback models with no timeout per model. Each OpenAI API call could hang for the default fetch timeout (~30s). With 4 fallback models, worst case is 2 minutes before the adapter's 20s timeout fires, producing a mismatch.

SpeechPlayer: AVAudioPlayer.stop() is documented to NOT call audioPlayerDidFinishPlaying. The guard at line 30 is correct for genuine finish events but provides no protection if a future iOS/macOS version changes this behavior (the guard would correctly prevent clearing a live player reference).
testing_gaps: No test for NSAlert orphaning during task cancellation — requires UI-level integration test or manual scenario documentation
No multi-monitor test for AugmentPanel positioning — tests use hardcoded frames, never exercise NSScreen resolution
No TTS response size boundary test — no test sends a large/malformed response body to verify memory safety
No test for LIVE WebSocket server errors after startup — existing tests only verify connection establishment
No test for processInvocation cancellation during confirmation await — the replay/race condition requires structured concurrency testing
AugmentPanel rapid-dismiss lifecycle test only covers single panel — no test creates 20+ panels to verify resource cleanup
